the-name.body:
The ​name is ‌attested in ‌Greek ​as **Σειρήν**. ​Etymologically ​it means ​"Binder, entangler"[^1].

​The ‌ASCII form ​*seiren* ​survives only ‌because the ​early ‌domain-name system ​could ‌not carry ​diacritics; it ​is ​a technological ​compromise, ​not an ‌ancient spelling. ​The ‌Unicode restoration ​**Seirḗn** ‌recovers both ​the stress ‌accent ​and the ‌vowel ​length of ​the original ‌directly ‌in the ‌address ​bar. The ​original carries ‌both ​stress and ​vowel ‌length, and ​exactly one ​historically ‌valid Unicode ​restoration ‌exists, which ​places the ​name ​in Tier ​1.

‌The letter-by-letter ‌transformation runs:

​- ‌**s** → ​**S** ​— S ‌uppercase
- ‌**e** ‌→ **e** ‌— ​e same
‌- **i** ​→ ​**i** — ​i ‌same
- ​**r** → ​**r** ​— r ‌same
​- **e** ​→ **ḗ** ​— ‌Stress + ​length
‌- **n** ​→ **n** ‌— ​n same

‌The ‌project holds ​the domain ​**seirḗn.com** ​(xn--seirn-yd1b.com) as ​the ‌canonical home ‌of this ​name[^2].

sources.citation: Odyssey.
Apollonius Rhodius.

overview.body:
**Seirḗn** ​(*seiren*) — ‌The ‌Song on ​the ​Rocks — ​belongs ​to the ​Greek ‌tradition, where ​it ​is catalogued ‌under ​the domain ‌"Enchanting ​Singer". The ‌name ​means "Binder, ​entangler"[^1].

​Seirḗn is ​the ​most intelligent ‌monster ​in the ‌Odyssey: ​she does ‌not ​promise pleasure ‌but ​knowledge — ‌"we ​know everything ​that ‌happens on ‌the ‌fruitful earth." ​The ​Greeks feared ‌her ​because her ​offer ‌is exactly ​what ​the wise ‌cannot ​refuse.[^2]

PuniCodex ‌restores ​the name ​as ​**Seirḗn** and ​serves ‌its temple ‌at ​[seirḗn.com](https://xn--seirn-yd1b.com). The ‌original ​carries both ​stress ‌and vowel ‌length, ‌and exactly ‌one ​historically valid ‌Unicode ​restoration exists, ​which ​places the ‌name ​in Tier ​1. ​The plain ‌ASCII ​form *seiren* ​survives ​as a ‌modern ​convenience imposed ‌by ​the early ‌domain-name ​system; the ‌restoration, ‌not the ​fallback, ​is the ​form ​the project ‌defends ‌as philologically ​complete[^3].

domains.body:
Seirḗn ​is ‌the most ‌intelligent ​monster ​in the ​Odyssey: ​she ​does ‌not promise ​pleasure ​but ‌knowledge — ​"we ‌know ​everything ‌that happens ​on ​the ​fruitful earth." ​The ​Greeks ‌feared ​her because ‌her ​offer ‌is exactly ​what ‌the ​wise ‌cannot refuse.[^1]

​### ​The ‌Song

Not ‌seduction ‌but ​information: ​the Sirens ‌sing ​the ​Trojan War ‌to ​the ​man ‌who fought ​it.

‌### ​The ​Mast

Odysseus ​bound, ​crew ‌deafened with ‌wax ​— ‌the ​original architecture ​of ‌resisting ‌temptation.

### ‌Orpheus' ‌Counter-Song

​The ‌Argonauts were ​saved ​not ​by wax ‌but ​by ​art: ​Orpheus out-sang ‌the ​Sirens ​themselves.

### ​Bird ‌and ​Maiden

‌The Greek ​form ‌— ​woman's head ‌on ‌a ​bird's ​body; the ​fishtail ​mermaid ‌is a ‌medieval ​graft.

syncretism.body:
Late ​antiquity ‌moralized ‌her: ​Christian ​writers ​made ​the Sirens ​the ‌seductions ​of ​the ‌world, ​the ‌mast ​the ‌cross. ​The ​Middle ​Ages ​merged ​her ‌with the ​fish-tailed ‌northern ​mermaid ‌— ​the ‌bird-maiden ​of ‌Greece ​becoming ​the ‌siren ‌of ‌romance ​— ​and French ‌gave ​the ​world ‌sirène, ​which ​is ‌why ​modern ‌alarm ​sirens ​and ​mermaids ​share ‌a word. ‌Kafka's ​parable ‌"The ​Silence ​of ‌the ‌Sirens" ‌gave ‌her ​the ‌last ​modern ​turn: ​a ‌more fatal ​weapon ​than ​song ‌is ​silence.[^1]

​Within ​the ‌Greek ​tradition, ‌closely ​related ‌names ​in ‌the ‌corpus include ​[[acheron|Achérōn]], ​[[achilleus|Achilleús]], ​[[adamas|Adámas]], ​[[aer|Aḗr]], ‌[[aither|Aithḗr]], ‌and ​[[ananke|Anánkē]].

oracle-sites.body: The ​Sirens' ‌geography ‌is ​the ​Odyssey's mapped ​onto ​real ​water: ‌the ​**Sirenusae** ​— ‌the ​Li ‌Galli ​islets off ‌the ​Sorrentine ​peninsula ​— ​were ​pointed ‌out ​to ‌Roman travelers ​as ‌their ​meadow, ‌and ​Strabo ‌records ​the ​local ‌traditions ‌of a ‌temple ​of ​Athēnā ‌on ​the ​cape ‌founded ​by ​Odysseus ‌himself. Their ​true ‌sanctuaries, ​however, ​were ​tombs: ​in ‌South ‌Italy, ​Sirens ‌were carved ​on ​funerary ‌monuments ‌as ‌musicians ‌of ​the ‌dead ​— ​the bird-maidens ​who ‌sing ​the ​soul ​across ‌the ​other, ​greater ​sea. The ‌British ​Museum's ‌famous ​Odysseus ‌stamnos ​and ‌the ‌Paestum ​tomb-paintings ​preserve this ​cult ​face ‌of ‌the ​enchantresses.

sources.citation: Strabo 5.4.8; on funerary Sirens, see the South Italian tomb corpora.

mythology.body:
Daughters of ​the river-god Achelōos and ‌a Muse — Melpomenē ‌or Terpsichorē in ​the later accounts — ​the Seirḗnes unite ​the authority of water ​and the authority of ​song.[^1]

### Odyssey ‌12 (The Passage)

Kirkē ​warns Odysseus: the Sirens ​"enchant all who ‌come near," and their ​island is heaped with ‌bones. He has ​his crew plug their ‌ears with wax ​and lash him to ​the mast. The Sirens ​hail him by ​name — they know ​his story — and ‌promise that whoever ​hears them sails away ‌"wiser." He strains at ​the ropes; the ‌ship passes; the danger ​is measured in ‌the distance of a ​song.[^2]

### Out-Sung by ‌Orpheus (The Contest)

​Apollonius Rhodius sends the ​Argonauts past the same ‌shore: one crewman, ‌Boutēs, leaps overboard in ‌surrender, but Orpheus strikes ​his lyre and ​drowns the enchantment in ‌a nobler song. ​Later tradition completes the ​logic — defeated by ‌Odysseus or Orpheus, ​the Sirens throw themselves ​into the sea and ‌become rocks: a ​song that fails to ‌bind has no reason ​to exist.

### ​The Lost Wings (The ​Plaint)

In Euripides' ​Helen and later lyric, ‌the Sirens are mourners: ‌they searched the ​world for the abducted ‌Persephonē and were given ​— or kept ​— their wings for ‌the search. It is ‌the myth behind ‌the monster: grief transformed ‌into inquiry, the ​song that asks after ‌the lost girl forever.

​### Companions of ​Persephonē (The Maidens)

The ​fullest genealogy makes them ‌the girlhood companions ​of Persephonē: they were ​playing with her in ​the meadow when ‌Hádēs struck, and they ​asked the gods ​for wings to search ​the world for her. ‌In Ovid's telling ​their transformation is their ‌answer to failure — ​half bird, half ‌maiden forever, still calling ​across the sea for ‌the lost girl. ‌The myth explains everything ​about them: the ​song that stops ships ​is a search that ​never ended, and ‌the sailors it kills ‌are drowned in someone ​else's grief.

meditation.body:
Seirḗn is ​the patroness ‌of dangerous ‌knowledge — ​the truth ​that costs ​the listener ​his course. ​The Greeks' ‌answer was ​not ignorance ​but engineering: hear ‌the song, ​keep the ‌ropes. Her ​question remains ‌the sharpest ​in the ​Odyssey: if ​a voice ​offered to ​tell you ‌everything, could you ​sail past ‌it?

Her ​question has ‌only sharpened ​in the ‌age of ​the infinite ‌song. Every ​feed is ​the meadow ‌now — a ‌voice that ‌knows your ​name, your ​war, your ‌wants, and ​promises wisdom ​if you ‌only stop ​rowing. The ​Odyssey's answer ‌was never ignorance: ​hear everything, ‌keep the ​ropes, and ​let your ​crew row ​deaf through ‌the meadow ‌of bones. ​Attention is ‌the last ​navigable strait, and ​she still ‌sings on ‌both shores ‌of it.

‌Notice what ​the myth ‌never does: ​it never ​silences them. ​The Greeks ‌kept the song ​on their ​vases, their ​tombs, their ‌stages — ​the danger ​preserved in ​full voice, ‌ropes and ​all. That ‌is the ​tradition's real instruction: ‌do not ​destroy the ‌enchantment, bind ‌yourself honestly ​to your ​course, and ​let the ​singing continue. ‌Some knowledge ‌is only ​safe underway.[^1]

sources.citation: Homer, Iliad / Odyssey, Loeb Classical Library / Oxford Classical Texts, 750 BCE.

homeric-hymns.body: The ​corpus ‌contains ‌no ​hymn ​to the ​Seirḗnes ​— ​fittingly: ‌their ​own ​song ‌is ​the ‌only ​one they ‌have. ​Their ​hymnic ​presence ​is ​the ‌Odyssey's, ​which ‌reports the ​song's ‌opening ​lines ‌("Come ​here, ‌renowned ​Odysseus, ​great ‌glory ‌of the ‌Achaeans") ​and ​so ‌preserves ​antiquity's ​most ‌quoted ​specimen ​of ‌enchantment. Later ​tradition ‌gives ​them ​parents ​from ​the ‌hymnic ‌world ​— ‌a Muse ​for ​a ‌mother ‌— ‌and ‌Euripides' ​*Helen* ‌(167–178) ​gives ​them their ​one ‌tragic ​aria, ​the ​invocation ‌to ​the ​winged ​maidens to ‌join ​her ‌lament. ​It ‌is ​the ‌closest ‌Greek ​tragedy ​comes to ​letting ​them ‌sing ‌on ​stage.

pronunciation.body:
The ​reconstructed ‌pronunciation ‌of ​the ​name ​is **/sɛː.rɛ̌ːn/** ​— ​Attic ‌Greek.[^1]

​For ​the ‌modern ​speaker, ‌the ​closest ‌approximation ​is: say-RAIN, ​stacked ​macron+acute ​on ​the ‌final ​ē.

‌Kindred ​and ‌historical ​forms ‌of the ​name:

‌- ​**Greek** ​— ‌Σειρήν
‌- ‌**Latin** ​— ​Siren
‌- ​**French** — ​sirène
‌- ​**Owned ​form** ‌— ​Seirḗn

‌Greek ​Σειρήν ​carries ​the ​accent on ‌the ‌final ​syllable ‌— ​Seirḗn ​— ‌and ‌the ‌etymology ‌is ​contested: folk ‌tradition ​heard ​σεῖρα, ​"cord," ‌for ​the ​binding ​song, ‌while ​modern ​scholarship looks ​to ‌Semitic ​or ‌pre-Greek ​roots. ‌The ​macron ‌on ‌the ​eta ​preserves the ​long ​vowel ‌of ‌the ​nominative.
